title: Searching for the ox
hook: the ten oxherding pictures: first, a herdsman searches for a lost ox

segments.voice: Yesterday, Huineng's teaching that meditation and wisdom are one. Your line: the lamp and its light. What did your one steady pause let you see? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-one.

A man stands at the edge of a field of wild grass, a rope in his hand. The grass is high. Beyond it, a river, and past the river, mountains. Somewhere out there is his ox, and it's gone. He starts walking. He pushes through the grass, crosses the water, climbs, and keeps going until the paths blur together and his legs give out. Evening comes. Nothing. No ox, no hoofprint, just cicadas in the trees as the light goes. That's the whole of the first picture. Today we begin a series of pictures that Chan and Zen have used to draw the way itself: searching for the ox.
screen: `A MAN WITH A ROPE.` → `GRASS, RIVER, MOUNTAINS.` → `ONLY CICADAS AT DUSK.`

segments.voice: First, the series. The oxherding pictures this path follows are a set of ten images, each with a short prose preface and a short poem. Tradition credits this set to a Chan teacher named Kuoan, known in Japan as Kakuan. They follow a herdsman and his ox from loss, through finding and taming, all the way home and beyond. Over the coming days we'll walk them one at a time. Second, the first picture. In paraphrase, the poem says: busily parting the endless grasses, he searches. The rivers are wide, the mountains far, the path keeps going. Worn out, he finds nothing, and hears only the cicadas in the evening maples. It is a picture of effort with no result yet. Third, the twist, in the preface. In paraphrase, it says: the ox has never gone missing. So why search? Because the herdsman turned his back on awakening, the ox became a stranger to him, and it got lost in the dust. Far from home, he stands at a crossroads, and gain and loss flare up in him like fire, right and wrong like a thicket of spears. Some readers hear the ox as the herdsman's own true nature: never really gone, only turned away from. Fourth, why the series starts here. It would be easy to skip this picture, to want the finding. But the first step is admitting the search is on, and naming it. In the pictures, everything that follows begins with someone out in the grass, looking.
screen: `A SERIES OF TEN PICTURES.` · `THE FIRST: ALONE IN TALL GRASS.` · `THE OX WAS NEVER LOST.` · `THE SEARCH, NAMED.` · then, large: `SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit and let the breath settle. Ask yourself, gently: what am I searching for? Not the polished answer. The real one. It might be peace, or approval, or rest, or something without a name yet. When it comes, name it simply, in a word or two, and don't argue with it. Then let the question go and just rest with the breath, the way the herdsman might finally sit down at dusk and listen to the cicadas. The bell holds the time.
Searching for the ox. The first of the oxherding pictures: a herdsman alone in the grasses, looking for an ox the preface says was never lost. Today's word.
Your line: searching. Today, when you catch yourself restless or reaching, pause and name what you're searching for. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Some Zen and Chan teachers use the oxherding pictures in talks and retreats as a map of practice, and students often study the pictures, prefaces and poems one stage at a time.

original.note: Chinese (xun niu): 'searching for the ox', the title of the first picture.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a farmer who lost an animal.
what it means: the first of a set of pictures of the way: someone searching hard for what, the preface says, was never lost.
what a scholar hears: the preface turns the search around: the ox only seems lost because the herdsman turned his back on awakening (背覺).

sources.ref: Ten Oxherding Pictures, picture 1 (preface and verse), attributed to Kuoan Shiyuan

notes: 'A set of ten' follows the Kuoan series being cited; other sets differ. Attribution to Kuoan (Kakuan) is framed as tradition's.

Check the paraphrase of the first preface (ox never lost; the herdsman turned his back on himself; lost in the dust; crossroads; gain and loss like fire, right and wrong like spears) and verse (endless grasses, wide rivers, far mountains, exhausted, cicadas in the evening maples).
'Some readers hear the ox as true nature' is interpretive and attributed; Keeper to confirm.

Editor pass: 'alone' is not in Kuoan's verse (忙忙撥草, busily parting the grasses) and 'turned his back on himself' now follows the preface's 背覺, turned his back on awakening; dropped 'widely used' and the claim that the set is simply 'ten' in general; replaced a closing line that folded Huineng and the Xinxin Ming into the herdsman's search with one that stays with the pictures.
